patient.name: Renata Cole
patient.chiefComplaint: Struck by vehicle, severe chest and body pain

history.hpi: Bystanders report the patient was crossing an intersection when she was struck by a sedan traveling an estimated 40 mph; she was thrown approximately 15 feet and landed on the pavement. On arrival she is awake, in severe distress, complaining of chest and left flank pain, with visibly paradoxical movement of the left lateral chest wall with each breath. Denies loss of consciousness per bystanders, though she is disoriented to time.
history.events: Struck by a vehicle while crossing an intersection; thrown roughly 15 feet on impact

scene.dispatch: 52-year-old female, pedestrian struck by vehicle, conscious, intersection
scene.location: Urban intersection, patient supine on pavement near the crosswalk, vehicle stopped nearby with a shattered windshield
scene.safety: Scene secured by police, traffic diverted; patient in the roadway near the curb lane
scene.bystanders: Multiple witnesses report the vehicle was traveling at high speed and did not brake before impact; patient was thrown approximately 15 feet
visualCues: Patient supine on pavement, visibly in distress
Paradoxical inward movement of the left lateral chest wall with each breath
Bruising and abrasions across the left chest and flank
Deformity of the left lower leg
Shattered windshield on the involved vehicle consistent with head/torso impact

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 52-year-old female pedestrian struck by a vehicle at high speed, thrown approximately 15 feet. She is alert but tachypneic and in severe pain, with visible paradoxical movement of the left chest wall consistent with a flail segment.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in short phrases due to pain
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, shallow, paradoxical inward movement of left lateral chest wall on inspiration
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present but rapid, skin pale and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities, guarding left chest and left lower leg
otherFindings: Paradoxical chest wall movement over the left lateral ribs
Left chest and flank bruising with tenderness on palpation
Deformity of the left lower leg, distal pulses intact
Disoriented to time, oriented to person and place
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It hurts... I can't breathe right... please help me."

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform MARCH primary survey: hemorrhage, airway, breathing, circulation, head/hypothermia
expectedActions.rationale: Structured survey rapidly identifies the life-threatening flail chest and rules out tension pneumothorax before other injuries are addressed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Palpate chest wall for instability/crepitus; auscultate breath sounds bilaterally
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Chest – See Initial Treatment: Palpate for instability/crepitus. Listen to breath sounds. Inspect for penetrating or soft tissue injuries
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms the flail segment and rules out an evolving tension pneumothorax before it becomes hemodynamically significant.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply high-flow supplemental oxygen to target SpO2 greater than 94%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor oxygen saturation (SpO2) and, if indicated, provide supplemental oxygen to maintain SPO2 greater than 94% and respiratory support if needed
expectedActions.rationale: Hypoxia from the flail segment and underlying pulmonary contusion requires immediate correction.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply cervical collar and initiate spinal motion restriction for distracting injuries
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Place patient in cervical collar and initiate spinal motion restriction in adults if there are any of the following: Another severe or painful distracting injury
expectedActions.rationale: The severe chest and leg injuries meet SMR criteria as distracting injuries even without a specific neck complaint.

transitions.condition: Crew performs a MARCH primary survey, identifies the flail segment and hypoxia, applies supplemental oxygen, and initiates spinal motion restriction given the severe distracting chest and leg injuries.
Crew moves on to splinting and transport without reassessing breath sounds; an evolving tension pneumothorax on the injured side goes unrecognized until the patient rapidly deteriorates.

phases.name: Primary survey and SMR completed
phases.description: Crew completes the MARCH primary survey, applies high-flow oxygen for hypoxia, palpates the chest wall confirming flail segment without tracheal deviation or absent breath sounds, and initiates cervical collar and spinal motion restriction given the severe distracting injuries.
phases.triggerCondition: After the massive-hemorrhage and airway checks are clear, the crew's breathing assessment confirms paradoxical chest wall movement without signs of tension pneumothorax; the severe, painful chest and leg injuries meet spinal motion restriction criteria as distracting injuries.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, paradoxical left chest wall movement persists, breath sounds present bilaterally, no tracheal deviation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid, IV access established
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities, guarding left chest and left lower leg
otherFindings: Cervical collar applied for spinal motion restriction
IV access established in right forearm
Chest wall instability and crepitus confirmed on palpation, no tracheal deviation
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "The oxygen helps a little... my chest still hurts so bad."

expectedActions.shortAction: 500 mL crystalloid IV bolus for HR >120 bpm; reassess and repeat as needed
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If SBP less than 90 mmHg or HR greater than 120 BPM, initiate resuscitation: consider 500 mL bolus of IV fluid, repeat as needed for persistent signs and symptoms of shock
expectedActions.rationale: Persistent tachycardia above 120 bpm meets the protocol's resuscitation threshold even with a normal systolic blood pressure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Fentanyl 70 mcg IV (70 kg × 1 mcg/kg; max initial dose 100 mcg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Fentanyl: 1 mcg/kg IN, IM, IV or IO (maximum initial dose of 100 mcg)
expectedActions.rationale: Severe pain (9/10) from the flail chest and leg injury warrants weight-based opioid analgesia.

transitions.condition: Given the persistent tachycardia above 120 bpm, crew initiates a 500 mL crystalloid bolus per resuscitation criteria and administers weight-based fentanyl for severe pain.

phases.name: Fluid bolus and fentanyl given
phases.description: Crew initiates a 500 mL crystalloid bolus for persistent tachycardia and administers weight-based fentanyl for severe pain, reassessing vitals and pain score after each intervention.
phases.triggerCondition: With HR persistently above 120 bpm meeting resuscitation criteria and pain remaining severe, the crew starts a fluid bolus and administers fentanyl, reassessing the response.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved tidal volume, paradoxical movement less pronounced with positioning
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses stronger, skin warming slightly
otherFindings: Left lower leg splinted in position found
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That's a lot better, thank you. I can breathe a little easier."

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and breath sounds serially en route; monitor for delayed tension pneumothorax
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Repeat primary assessment or secondary assessment should be conducted en route to the trauma center. If patient develops difficulty with ventilation, reassess breath sounds for development of tension pneumothorax
expectedActions.rationale: Flail chest and pulmonary contusion can decompensate en route even after initial stabilization.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to appropriate trauma center per field triage guideline; minimize scene time
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Decisions regarding transport destination should be based on the ACS-COT 2022 National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients
expectedActions.rationale: High-speed pedestrian-struck mechanism with multi-system trauma warrants transport to the highest level of trauma care.

transitions.condition: With pain controlled and perfusion improving, the patient is packaged and prepared for rapid transport with serial reassessment en route.

phases.name: Reassessed and prepared for transport
phases.description: Patient is packaged with spinal motion restriction, splinted leg, oxygen, and IV access, and transported with continued serial reassessment given the multi-system mechanism.
phases.triggerCondition: After fluid and pain management, the patient's perfusion and comfort have improved; crew initiates rapid transport with ongoing serial vital sign monitoring.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved, mild residual paradoxical movement with deep breaths
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial and pedal pulses strong bilaterally
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities, sensation intact distal to splinted leg
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel more comfortable now. How much longer to the hospital?"

phases.name: Chest reassessment skipped
phases.description: Without ongoing chest reassessment, an evolving tension pneumothorax on the injured side goes unrecognized. The patient rapidly decompensates with absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, and hypotension, requiring emergent needle decompression.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew proceeds to splinting and transport without reassessing breath sounds after the initial survey; the flail segment's underlying lung injury progresses to tension pneumothorax unrecognized until the patient decompensates.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Severely labored, absent breath sounds on the left, tracheal deviation to the right
otherFindings: Absent breath sounds on the left

expectedActions.shortAction: Needle decompression of left chest for tension pneumothorax with hypotension and tracheal deviation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If absent or diminished breath sounds in a hypotensive trauma patient, especially those with chest trauma and/or tracheal deviation, consider tension pneumothorax and perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation; may need second or third needle decompression on same side if there is a rush of air but patient again has symptoms
expectedActions.rationale: Absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, JVD, and hypotension are classic signs of tension pneumothorax requiring emergent decompression.
